verdict.rationale: At Pentecost the noun "language or dialect" (dialektos, Strong's G1258) in Acts 2:6 and 2:8 denotes a specific spoken language, with the relative clause "into which we were born" (en hei egennethemen) anchoring it to the mother tongue, and the ethnic catalogue of Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and Arabs makes the real-human-language reading lexically secure for that scene. The other noun "tongue" (glossa, Strong's G1100) is used interchangeably with "language" (dialektos) in Acts 2:11, equating the two terms there. But in 1 Corinthians 14:2 the same "tongue" (glossa) is paired with "he speaks not to men but to God" (ouk anthropois lalei alla theoi), "no one hears or understands" (oudeis akouei), and "he speaks mysteries" (mysteria lalei), and 1 Corinthians 14:27 requires an "interpreter" (diermeneutes, Strong's G1329) rather than a translator. 1 Corinthians 13:1 even contemplates "tongues of men and of angels" (glossais ton anthropon kai ton aggelon), extending the category beyond ordinary human speech. Because the proposition asserts one unified definition of the biblical gift while the lexical data splits into an immediately-intelligible-witness pattern in Acts and a needs-interpretation, directed-to-God pattern in 1 Corinthians, with the same lexeme (the same underlying Greek word) bearing apparently different referents, the verdict is disputed: the Pentecost-bound clause is well supported, but the canon-wide identity claim is materially contested at the lexical level.

scripture.reasoning: The disciples begin to speak "in other tongues" (heterais glossais) as the Spirit gave them "to utter, declare" (apophthengesthai). The adjective "other" (heterais) marks the tongues as other than their own, and the immediately following narrative identifies those others as the native languages of the assembled nations.

Each one "kept hearing" (ekouon) the disciples "speaking" (lalounton) "in his own language" (tei idiai dialektoi). The noun "language" (dialektos) here names a definite spoken human tongue, and the distributive "his own" (idiai) ties each hearer to his particular native speech, which fixes the Pentecost phenomenon as real-language communication received as intelligible.

The crowd asks how each "we hear" (akouomen) "in our own language into which we were born" (tei idiai dialektoi hemon en hei egennethemen). The relative clause "into which we were born" (en hei egennethemen) anchors "language" (dialektos) to the mother tongue of birth, which is the strongest lexical signal that Pentecost tongues were genuine ethnic languages, not non-cognitive utterance (speech that does not carry meaning the mind processes). The noun "language" (dialektos) has six total New Testament occurrences (Acts 1:19, 2:6, 2:8, 21:40, 22:2, 26:14) and in every one denotes a real spoken human language, never ecstatic speech (excited, non-rational utterance).

The hearers say "we hear them speaking in our own tongues" (akouomen lalounton auton tais hemeterais glossais) "the great works of God" (the megaleia tou theou). Here "tongues" (glossais) is used interchangeably with "languages" (dialektoi) of verses 6 and 8, equating the two terms within the same pericope (the same connected passage) and confirming that the content was intelligible proclamation of God's deeds.

Paul writes "if I speak in the tongues of men and of angels" (ean tais glossais ton anthropon lalo kai ton aggelon). The coordinated genitive "of angels" (ton aggelon, a noun in the 'of-X' grammatical form), joined to "of men" (ton anthropon) by "and" (kai), extends the category of "tongue" (glossa) beyond ordinary human speech to a class denominated by angelic speakers. The construction is hypothetical ("if," ean, an 'if-then' clause), so it does not by itself prove a non-human category is the Corinthian phenomenon, but it shows the Pauline use of "tongue" (glossa) is not lexically restricted to ordinary human tongues.

The one "speaking in a tongue speaks not to men but to God" (lalon glossei ouk anthropois lalei alla theoi), "for no one understands" (oudeis gar akouei), "but by the spirit he speaks mysteries" (pneumati de lalei mysteria). Three lexical signals diverge sharply from the Acts 2 pattern: speech directed to God not to people, no human comprehension, and the content described as "mysteries" (mysteria). At Pentecost the same root "tongue" (glossa) is paired with immediate hearing in one's own "language" (dialektos), so this verse is the principal locus (the main place) where the canon-wide identity of "tongue" (glossa) fractures.

Paul says there are perhaps "so many kinds of languages" (tosauta gene phonon) in the world, "and none without meaning or sound" (kai ouden aphonon). The vocabulary of "sound or language" (phone) and "without sound or meaning" (aphonos) shows Paul reasoning from the model of actual human languages, which is consistent with a real-language frame and supplies the analogy he then applies to the Corinthian gift.

If I do not know "the force of the language" (dynamis tes phones), I will be "a foreigner" (barbaros) to the speaker and he "a foreigner" (barbaros) to me. The noun "foreigner" (barbaros) is the technical term for one whose speech is an unintelligible foreign language, which both supports the real-language analogy and shows that in Corinth the tongue functioned as unintelligible to the hearer absent comprehension, a different effect from the immediate hearing at Pentecost.

If anyone "speaks in a tongue" (lalei glossei), let it be by two or at most three, "and in turn" (kai ana meros), and let one "interpret" (diermeneueto). The verb "to interpret" (diermeneuo, Strong's G1329) is used here, not just "to explain" (hermeneuo) alone, the same compound that elsewhere renders Hebrew or Aramaic into Greek (compare Luke 24:27, Acts 9:36); its presence is compatible with both a translation and an explanatory rendering, but the requirement of such a mediator shows that in the Corinthian assembly the tongue was not automatically understood by hearers as at Pentecost.

If there is no "interpreter" (diermeneutes), let the speaker "keep silent" (sigato) in the assembly, and let him speak "to himself and to God" (heautoi kai toi theoi). The directed-to-God communicative aim, with the speech silenced in public when uninterpreted, contrasts with the public intelligible witness of Acts 2 and is the lexical crux (the key word-level decision-point) that divides the readings.

Paul cites the Isaiah text "in other tongues and in lips of others I will speak to this people" (en heteroglossois kai en cheilesin heteron laleso toi laoi toutoi). The compound "other-tongued" (heteroglossos) and the parallel "lips of others" (cheilesin heteron) describe foreign-language speech as a sign to unbelieving Israel, which leans the Corinthian gift toward real human languages and partially harmonizes it with Acts 2.

complicating_texts.resolution: The clause "the one speaking in a tongue speaks not to men but to God" (ho gar lalon glossei ouk anthropois lalei alla theoi) describes a communicative direction toward God rather than the human audience addressed at Pentecost, and the added clauses "no one understands" (oudeis akouei) and "he speaks mysteries in spirit" (pneumati de lalei mysteria) describe content that is opaque to hearers. The same noun "tongue" (glossa) is used as in Acts 2, but the function differs: at Pentecost the speech is heard by men in their native "language" (dialektos) as intelligible witness, while in Corinth the uninterpreted tongue is not understood by men. This is the principal reason the canon-wide identity of the gift is contested, so it is recorded as the driver of the disputed verdict rather than as a resolved harmonization.

Paul's statement that when he prays "in a tongue" (glossei) his "spirit" (pneuma) prays but his "mind" (nous) is "unfruitful" (akarpos) indicates that the speaker himself does not cognitively process the content. This is compatible with speaking a real but personally-unlearned language whose meaning the speaker does not consciously parse, yet it is also read by some as non-cognitive utterance (speech that bypasses rational understanding), so the lexical data underdetermines the choice and the verdict remains disputed.

The phrase "tongues of men and of angels" (tais glossais ton anthropon kai ton aggelon) is hypothetical ("if," ean, an 'if-then' construction) and rhetorical, so it does not by itself establish that the Corinthian gift includes angelic speech, but the very availability of the angelic category within the Pauline use of "tongue" (glossa) shows the lexeme (the underlying Greek word) is not lexically restricted to ordinary human tongues. Whether the speaker meant a real but heavenly language or a non-translatable spiritual utterance is exactly what the words do not decide, which is why the proposition's universal claim is underdetermined.

variants.note: No CBGM-published (Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, the current scholarly system for evaluating New Testament textual variants) variant units cover Acts 2 or 1 Corinthians 13 to 14 in scope. The minor apparatus markers visible in the bundle (for example the diairesis, a mark indicating separate pronunciation, at "to utter" (apophthengesthai) in Acts 2:4 and small readings in 1 Corinthians 14:10) do not alter the lexical sense of "tongue" (glossa), "language" (dialektos), "mystery" (mysterion), or "to interpret" (diermeneuo), so the verdict holds across plausible variant readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Treats "language" (dialektos) in Acts 2:6 and 2:8 as the controlling term, reads "tongue" (glossa) in 1 Corinthians 14 as the same real-language gift heard as a foreign tongue, and points to "foreigner" (barbaros) in 1 Corinthians 14:11 and the "other-tongued" (heteroglossos) quotation of Isaiah 28:11 in 1 Corinthians 14:21 as Pauline confirmation that the Corinthian phenomenon is foreign human language. Reads 1 Corinthians 14:2 "he speaks to God" (lalei theoi) as descriptive of the situation where no native speaker is present to hear, not as defining the gift's essence.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: two-phenomena (real in Acts, distinct in Corinth)
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Holds that "language" (dialektos) plus the named nations fix the Pentecost phenomenon as real human languages for intelligible witness, while 1 Corinthians 14:2 ("he speaks to God" lalei theoi, "no one understands" oudeis akouei, "mysteries" mysteria), 14:14 ("the mind is unfruitful," nous akarpos), 14:27 to 28 (requires an "interpreter" diermeneutes else silence), and the hypothetical "angel" (aggelos) in 13:1 describe a different gift directed to God whose content is opaque to hearers. On this reading "tongue" (glossa) is polysemous (carrying more than one distinct meaning) across the two corpora and the proposition's unified definition is materially contested.

Treats "tongue" (glossa) as non-translatable spiritual utterance even at Pentecost, reading "language" (dialektos) as referring to the hearers' miracle of perception rather than the speakers' content (the miracle in the ear, not in the mouth). Cites "he speaks to God" (lalei theoi), "unfruitful mind" (nous akarpos), "mysteries" (mysteria), and "in tongues of angels" (tais glossais ton aggelon) as defining the category, and reads Acts 2's catalogue of nations as a divine sign rather than a description of the speech itself.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on whether "tongue" (glossa) in 1 Corinthians 13 to 14 is lexically identical to "tongue" (glossa) equated with "language" (dialektos) in Acts 2:6 to 2:11. The grammatico-historical data (the meaning derived from grammar plus original-context history) secures the Pentecost clause but leaves the canon-wide identity open, which is why three defensible lenses produce divergent verdicts. All three are recorded in their strongest lexical form so a reader holding any of them sees the position represented fairly.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What is the lexical referent of "tongue" (glossa) and "language" (dialektos) in the Pentecost narrative of Acts 2, and does that referent extend without remainder to "tongue" (glossa) as used in 1 Corinthians 13 to 14?
stem_audit.notes: The proposition embeds a conclusion in three places: it asserts the gift is real human languages, asserts the languages are previously unknown to the speaker, and asserts the purpose is intelligible witness. The neutralized form asks the lexical question without presupposing the answer. The verdict was derived on the original stem; the audit confirms that the Pentecost portion is lexically supported while the universalizing claim that the same definition governs 1 Corinthians 14 is the contested element.

lay_summary: Two Greek words carry this question. In the Pentecost account in Acts 2 the crowd hears the disciples speaking and each one hears in his own "language" (dialektos), the noun for a specific spoken language or native dialect. Acts 2:8 anchors it tightly by adding "into which we were born" (en hei egennethemen), and the listed nations, Parthians, Medes, Elamites, people from Egypt, Asia, Crete, and Arabia, show these were real ethnic languages. The content was the great works of God, heard and understood on the spot. Across all six times "language" (dialektos) appears in the New Testament it always names a real spoken human language, never ecstatic speech (excited, non-rational utterance). In Acts 2:11 the other word, "tongue" (glossa), is used as an equivalent. For that scene the words clearly point to genuine human languages spoken for intelligible witness. The difficulty comes when the same word "tongue" (glossa) appears in 1 Corinthians. There Paul says the one speaking in a tongue speaks not to men but to God, that no one understands him, that he speaks "mysteries" (mysteria) by the spirit, and that his own mind is unfruitful. He also requires an "interpreter" (diermeneutes), and if none is present the speaker must stay silent and speak only to himself and God. In 1 Corinthians 13:1 he even contemplates tongues of men and of angels. He does reach for foreign-language vocabulary, using the word "foreigner" (barbaros) for one whose speech you cannot understand, and quoting the prophet about other tongues, which leans toward real languages. But the directed-to-God aim, the no-one-understands, the mysteries, and the angels phrase pull the other way. So the words themselves strongly support the real-language and intelligible-witness reading for Pentecost, yet they do not settle whether the very same definition governs the Corinthian gift. Because the proposition asserts one unified definition across the whole canon, and the lexical evidence splits between an immediately understood pattern in Acts and a needs-interpretation pattern in 1 Corinthians, the overall picture is genuinely contested at the level of the words, rather than plainly established or plainly denied.
